Covariance Structure and Coordinate Heterogeneity
Govern Binary Quantization of Contrastive Embeddings

Wenxuan Xiao Affiliation: Changsha University Email: daflyflowers@gmail.com
Abstract

Binary quantization (BQ) compresses high-dimensional embeddings into one or two bits per coordinate, enabling nearest neighbor search at extreme speed. Yet a striking puzzle persists: BQ achieves competitive recall on contrastive embeddings but fails on others—and two leading systems adopt diametrically opposite strategies (random rotation vs. preserving coordinate axes) without a common theory explaining when each is appropriate.

We address this puzzle by connecting the Gaussian structure recently established for InfoNCE-trained representations to a statistical framework for BQ quality. Our analysis reveals two distinct roles of the covariance matrix Σ\Sigma. First, the full covariance structure—not merely its diagonal—determines the absolute level of ranking fidelity, with off-diagonal correlations contributing 30–50% of the signal. Second, coordinate heterogeneity (the non-uniformity of per-coordinate variances) governs key design choices: how much each additional bit contributes, and whether random rotation helps or hurts. We derive approximate expressions for ranking fidelity under a Gaussian model, show that the magnitude bit carries information proportional to heterogeneity, and show that random rotation destroys precisely the signal that one paradigm exploits while creating the isotropy that the other requires. A phenomenological scaling law predicts fidelity across models and dimensions. Experiments on 18 datasets spanning 9 embedding families support the main predictions and provide, to our knowledge, the first principled design guide for binary quantization systems.

1 Introduction

A curious fact has emerged from the rapid adoption of vector search: binary quantization—an extreme form of compression, retaining just the sign of each coordinate—works remarkably well on embeddings produced by contrastive learning, yet performs poorly on embeddings from other training paradigms. Systems built on this observation have proliferated. QuIVer (Xiao et al., 2026) constructs its entire graph index in two-bit space; RaBitQ (Gao and Long, 2024) applies random rotation before binarization and corrects distances with per-vector scalars. These two designs make opposite assumptions about coordinate structure, yet both report competitive recall on contrastive embeddings (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019; Nussbaum et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024). Why does binary quantization work at all—and why do contradictory strategies both succeed?

The classical answer appeals to locality-sensitive hashing (LSH): random hyperplane projections preserve angular similarity (Indyk and Motwani, 1998; Charikar, 2002; Goemans and Williamson, 1995). But this theory assumes isotropic data and analyzes worst-case performance; it cannot explain the strong dependence on training objective that practitioners observe. The missing ingredient, we argue, is the specific distributional structure that contrastive training imposes on representations. Betser et al. (2026) recently proved that InfoNCE induces approximately Gaussian coordinate distributions—a result that transforms the question from geometry (“how are points arranged on the sphere?”) to statistics (“what does the covariance matrix look like?”).

Building on this Gaussian prior, we show that the full covariance structure Σ\Sigma—not merely its diagonal—determines ranking fidelity, and that coordinate heterogeneity (the non-uniformity of per-coordinate variances) governs the effectiveness of key design choices. Heterogeneity determines how much the magnitude bit adds (its gain is monotone in variance dispersion), and why rotation helps one system but hurts another (rotation equalizes variances, destroying the implicit weighting that Hamming distance exploits while creating the isotropy that linear correctors require). Concretely, we establish the following:

  • •

    An approximate Spearman fidelity formula via Stein’s lemma, revealing that off-diagonal covariance contributes 30–50% of ranking accuracy (§4, Theorem 1).

  • •

    A per-coordinate analysis showing that the magnitude bit is strictly more informative than the sign bit, with gain monotone in heterogeneity (§5, Proposition 5).

  • •

    A rotation–fidelity duality that unifies the QuIVer and RaBitQ design philosophies (§4.2, Theorem 2 and Corollaries 3–4).

  • •

    A phenomenological scaling law that predicts fidelity across models and dimensions from three covariance statistics (§6).

We validate every theoretical prediction on 18 datasets spanning 9 embedding families and dimensions from 100 to 3072, including a non-Gaussian control (GIST-960) that confirms the necessity of the Gaussian prior. In graph-based search, the two-bit advantage is amplified 1.2–4.1×\times in local neighborhoods—a phenomenon our framework explains through conditional concentration. The resulting framework provides, to our knowledge, the first principled explanation for why binary quantization succeeds on contrastive embeddings and concrete guidance for choosing between rotation-based and coordinate-preserving system designs.

2 Related Work

Binary quantization and LSH.

The theoretical foundation for binary encoding was laid by locality-sensitive hashing (Indyk and Motwani, 1998) and SimHash (Charikar, 2002), which connects Hamming distance to angular similarity via Pr[h(x)=h(y)]=1−arccos(cos(x,y))/π\Pr[h(x)=h(y)]=1-\arccos(\cos(x,y))/\pi. The semidefinite rounding analysis of Goemans and Williamson (1995) provides complementary guarantees. Crucially, these results assume isotropic data or analyze worst-case performance; they say nothing about how distributional structure—heterogeneous variances, non-trivial covariance—affects BQ quality. Our work shows that this structure is not merely present but is the dominant factor: ranking fidelity depends on the full covariance matrix, not just on dimension and angle.

Modern BQ systems.

Two recent systems illustrate the design tension that motivates our theory. RaBitQ (Gao and Long, 2024) rotates vectors to isotropy before binarization, then corrects distances with per-vector scalars, achieving an unbiased estimator with variance O⁡(1/D)O(1/D). QuIVer (Xiao et al., 2026) takes the opposite approach: it preserves coordinate axes and builds the entire graph index—edge selection, pruning, navigation—natively in two-bit space. Both build on graph-based ANN indices (Malkov and Yashunin, 2020; Subramanya et al., 2019; Aumüller et al., 2020) and both achieve competitive recall, yet they make contradictory assumptions about coordinate structure. RaBitQ provides universal error bounds via a distribution-free analysis, but does not exploit the specific structure of contrastive embeddings; QuIVer demonstrates strong empirical performance in coordinate-preserving mode, but does not explain its theoretical basis. Neither identifies the role of coordinate heterogeneity.

Contrastive representation structure.

The distributional structure we exploit originates in the InfoNCE objective (van den Oord et al., 2018), which balances alignment of positive pairs with uniformity pressure on the hypersphere (Wang and Isola, 2020; Chen and He, 2021). This framework underlies SimCLR (Chen et al., 2020), MoCo (He et al., 2020), CLIP (Radford et al., 2021), and has been studied through downstream guarantees (Saunshi et al., 2019), spectral analysis (HaoChen et al., 2021), and identifiability (Zimmermann et al., 2021). The key theoretical result we build on is due to Betser et al. (2026), who proved that InfoNCE induces asymptotically Gaussian coordinates under alignment plateau and thin-shell concentration, formalizing observations from DINO (Caron et al., 2021) and VICReg (Bardes et al., 2022). By contrast, neural collapse (Papyan et al., 2020) produces maximally isotropic supervised features—a qualitatively different regime. Isotropy-promoting methods (Ermolov et al., 2021; Bardes et al., 2022) regularize toward uniform variances but do not analyze what happens when residual heterogeneity remains. Our contribution is to show that this residual heterogeneity is not a defect but the signal that BQ exploits.

Vector quantization.

Product quantization (Jégou et al., 2011), optimized PQ (Ge et al., 2014), and ScaNN (Guo et al., 2020) operate in the 4–64 bit regime with learned codebooks, implemented efficiently in FAISS (Johnson et al., 2019). Our analysis targets the extreme 1–2 bit setting where no codebook is needed and distances reduce to hardware-accelerated popcount. The mathematical tools are also different: we rely on Stein’s lemma (Stein, 1981; Liu, 1994), Hoeffding’s inequality (Hoeffding, 1963), and high-dimensional concentration (Vershynin, 2018; Boucheron et al., 2013; Diaconis and Freedman, 1987), rather than rate-distortion or codebook design theory.

3 Preliminaries

3.1 Binary Quantization

Let x,y∈ℝDx,y\in\mathbb{R}^{D} be unit-normalized embeddings. The 1-bit BQ score is

S1​(x,y)=∑i=1Dsign⁡(xi)​sign⁡(yi),S_{1}(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^{D}\operatorname{sign}(x_{i})\operatorname{sign}(y_{i}), (1)

which equals D−2⋅dH​(sign⁡(x),sign⁡(y))D-2\cdot d_{H}(\operatorname{sign}(x),\operatorname{sign}(y)) where dHd_{H} is Hamming distance.

The 2-bit BQ score augments each sign with a magnitude bit mix=𝟏[|xi|>αx]m_{i}^{x}=\mathbf{1}[|x_{i}|>\alpha_{x}], where αx=1D​∑j|xj|\alpha_{x}=\frac{1}{D}\sum_{j}|x_{j}|:

S2​(x,y)=∑i=1D(1+mix)​(1+miy)​sign⁡(xi)​sign⁡(yi).S_{2}(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^{D}(1+m_{i}^{x})(1+m_{i}^{y})\operatorname{sign}(x_{i})\operatorname{sign}(y_{i}). (2)

3.2 From Fidelity to Recall: The FF/GG Decomposition

Search recall depends on two independent factors. The first is ranking fidelity F=ρSpearman​(Sb,⟨x,y⟩)F=\rho_{\text{Spearman}}(S_{b},\langle x,y\rangle), the Spearman correlation between BQ scores and true inner products over random pairs. FF measures how much noise quantization introduces into rankings.

The second factor is the semantic margin structure of the data. Let qq be a query, n1n_{1} its true nearest neighbor, and n2n_{2} a competitor. The true margin Δ=⟨q,n1⟩−⟨q,n2⟩\Delta=\langle q,n_{1}\rangle-\langle q,n_{2}\rangle determines how hard the ranking problem is, independent of quantization. We denote this gap structure GG.

The two factors combine through a sub-Gaussian pairwise error bound:

P⁡[pairwise misordering]≤exp⁡(−γb2​Δ22​σBQ,b2),P[\text{pairwise misordering}]\leq\exp\!\left(-\frac{\gamma_{b}^{2}\,\Delta^{2}}{2\,\sigma_{\text{BQ},b}^{2}}\right), (3)

where γb\gamma_{b} (the calibration slope, a function of FF) controls how faithfully BQ scores track true inner products, and σBQ,b2\sigma_{\text{BQ},b}^{2} is the BQ score noise variance. A union bound over K⁡(N−K)K(N-K) candidate pairs gives

P⁡[top-​K​ error]≤K⁡(N−K)​exp⁡(−cb​Δmin2).P[\text{top-}K\text{ error}]\leq K(N-K)\,\exp\!\left(-c_{b}\,\Delta_{\min}^{2}\right). (4)

This decomposition clarifies the scope of our theory: we analyze FF (the noise side) while treating GG (the signal side) as a property of the data distribution. Improving FF—through bitwidth, rotation, or system design—reduces BQ noise without requiring any change to the embedding model or data.

3.3 The Gaussian Prior (H1)

Assumption 1 (Coordinate Gaussianity).

Let g⁡(x)∈ℝDg(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{D} denote the encoder output before normalization, and f⁡(x)=g⁡(x)/‖g⁡(x)‖f(x)=g(x)/\|g(x)\| the unit-normalized embedding.

  1. (H1a)

    For any fixed kk coordinates I={i1,…,ik}I=\{i_{1},\ldots,i_{k}\}, dBL​(ℒ⁡(gI),ℒ⁡(ZI))≤εDd_{\mathrm{BL}}(\mathcal{L}(g_{I}),\mathcal{L}(Z_{I}))\leq\varepsilon_{D} where Z∼𝒩⁡(μ,Σ)Z\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma).

  2. (H1b)

    There exists a deterministic rD>0r_{D}>0 such that 𝔼⁡[|‖g‖−rD|]/rD≤δD\mathbb{E}[|\|g\|-r_{D}|]/r_{D}\leq\delta_{D} and 𝔼⁡[|‖Z‖−rD|]/rD≤δD\mathbb{E}[|\|Z\|-r_{D}|]/r_{D}\leq\delta_{D}, with δD→0\delta_{D}\to 0.

H1a is a finite-dimensional marginal Gaussianity condition: it asserts that any fixed kk coordinates are approximately joint Gaussian, but does not require the full DD-dimensional distribution to be Gaussian. This is justified by Betser et al. (2026), who prove that InfoNCE induces asymptotically Gaussian coordinate distributions. H1b is a separate thin-shell concentration condition on the norm ‖g‖\|g\|; for Gaussian ZZ, it holds whenever the effective rank tr⁡(Σ)/‖Σ‖op→∞\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)/\|\Sigma\|_{\text{op}}\to\infty. Together, H1a provides the distributional structure used in Stein’s lemma and the sign/magnitude analysis, while H1b ensures that L2 normalization does not distort the coordinate-level statistics. We empirically verify both conditions across 13 datasets and 7 embedding models, finding QQ-plot R2≥0.9959R^{2}\geq 0.9959 (testing H1a) and norm CV ≤0.09\leq 0.09 (testing H1b) in all cases.

Roadmap.

Figure 1 summarizes the logical structure of our framework. The Gaussian prior (H1) connects the training objective to the covariance matrix Σ\Sigma, whose structure decomposes into heterogeneity (governing FF) and semantic margins (GG). Our theorems analyze the FF branch; GG is treated as given.

4 Ranking Fidelity Under the Gaussian Model

4.1 Stein’s Lemma and the Off-Diagonal Structure of FF

Theorem 1 (Linear covariance formula).

Under Assumption 1, let Z∼𝒩⁡(μ,Σ)Z\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma), S0=∑isign⁡(Zi)S_{0}=\sum_{i}\operatorname{sign}(Z_{i}), and T0=∑jdj​ZjT_{0}=\sum_{j}d_{j}Z_{j}. Define the Stein coefficient ai=2​φ​(μi/σi)/σia_{i}=2\varphi(\mu_{i}/\sigma_{i})/\sigma_{i}, where φ(t)=(2π)−1/2e−t2/2\varphi(t)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-t^{2}/2}. Then:

Cov⁡(S0,T0)=∑i,jai​Σi​j​dj.\operatorname{Cov}(S_{0},T_{0})=\sum_{i,j}a_{i}\,\Sigma_{ij}\,d_{j}. (5)

In particular, FF depends on the full covariance matrix Σ\Sigma, not just its diagonal.

The off-diagonal contribution to ranking quality is captured by the Stein squared signal:

ℐoff:=∑i≠j(ai​Σi​j)2=∑i≠jΣi​j2​4σi2​φ2​(μi/σi).\mathcal{I}_{\text{off}}:=\sum_{i\neq j}(a_{i}\Sigma_{ij})^{2}=\sum_{i\neq j}\Sigma_{ij}^{2}\frac{4}{\sigma_{i}^{2}}\varphi^{2}(\mu_{i}/\sigma_{i}). (6)

This is not Cov⁡(S0,T0)\operatorname{Cov}(S_{0},T_{0}) itself, but the Frobenius energy of the off-diagonal part of the Stein coefficient matrix (ai​Σi​j)i,j(a_{i}\Sigma_{ij})_{i,j}.

Weak correlations accumulate.

An important consequence of Eq. (6) is that off-diagonal contributions, though individually tiny (|ρi​j|≈0.04|\rho_{ij}|\approx 0.04–0.110.11), accumulate over D⁡(D−1)D(D-1) pairs. Under a dispersal condition 1D⁡(D−1)​∑i≠jρi​j2≍κ2/D\frac{1}{D(D-1)}\sum_{i\neq j}\rho_{ij}^{2}\asymp\kappa^{2}/D, the total off-diagonal Frobenius energy satisfies ∑i≠jρi​j2≍κ2​D\sum_{i\neq j}\rho_{ij}^{2}\asymp\kappa^{2}D, contributing a constant fraction (30–50%) of the total Stein signal. This D2D^{2} accumulation effect is the key reason why diagonal-only models systematically underestimate fidelity (Table 3).

Approximation budget.

Our framework involves three approximation steps, each with controlled error: (i) the Gaussian prior (Assumption 1, validated with R2>0.99R^{2}>0.99 across 13 datasets); (ii) the Pearson-to-Spearman conversion via Kruskal’s formula (exact for bivariate Gaussian, O⁡(ϵ)O(\epsilon) otherwise); and (iii) the mean-field closure (S0) used only in the scaling law (§6). The cumulative accuracy is validated end-to-end by the explanation ratios in Table 3 (mean 103%, residual MAE 0.024).

4.2 The Rotation Paradox

Theorem 2 (Rotation uniformizes coordinate variances).

Let QQ be a Haar-random orthogonal matrix. Then:

  1. (a)

    sign⁡(Q​x)\operatorname{sign}(Qx) defines a random-hyperplane LSH with P[h(x)=h(y)]=1−arccos(cos(x,y))/πP[h(x)=h(y)]=1-\arccos(\cos(x,y))/\pi.

  2. (b)

    maxi⁡|qi⊤​Σ​qi−tr⁡(Σ)/D|≲‖Σ‖op​log⁡D/D\max_{i}|q_{i}^{\top}\Sigma q_{i}-\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)/D|\lesssim\|\Sigma\|_{\text{op}}\sqrt{\log D/D}.

Corollary 3 (Rotation harms heterogeneity-aware BQ).

Rotation drives CV2​(σ)→0\mathrm{CV}^{2}(\sigma)\to 0 (Theorem 2b), eliminating the heterogeneity-dependent component Δhet\Delta_{\text{het}} of the 2-bit advantage (Proposition 5b). The residual gain Δ0>0\Delta_{0}>0 (the isotropic scalar magnitude advantage) survives, so 2-bit does not fully degrade to 1-bit; however, the data-dependent advantage that QuIVer exploits is destroyed.

Corollary 4 (Rotation helps linear-corrected BQ).

Uniformized SNR minimizes the estimation variance of the per-vector linear corrector d^=fadd+frescale×IP\hat{d}=f_{\text{add}}+f_{\text{rescale}}\times\text{IP}, since Var⁡(d^−d)∝(1−cos2⁡(r,x¯))/(D−1)\operatorname{Var}(\hat{d}-d)\propto(1-\cos^{2}(r,\bar{x}))/(D-1) is minimized at isotropy.

Proposition 5 (Per-coordinate magnitude gain and heterogeneity monotonicity).

In a simplified per-coordinate model under Assumption 1:

    Strict superiority. For each coordinate ii with σi>0\sigma_{i}>0, the per-dimension information ratio satisfies ηi(2):=(ai+bi)2/(1+3​pi)>ai2=:ηi(1)\eta_{i}^{(2)}:=(a_{i}+b_{i})^{2}/(1+3p_{i})>a_{i}^{2}=:\eta_{i}^{(1)}, where ai=σi​2/πa_{i}=\sigma_{i}\sqrt{2/\pi}, bi=2​σi​φ​(α/σi)b_{i}=2\sigma_{i}\varphi(\alpha/\sigma_{i}), and pi=erfc⁡(α/(σi​2))p_{i}=\operatorname{erfc}(\alpha/(\sigma_{i}\sqrt{2})). Remark 1 (Shared-threshold approximation).

In practice, the magnitude threshold αx=1D​∑j|xj|\alpha_{x}=\frac{1}{D}\sum_{j}|x_{j}| is shared across coordinates, introducing cross-coordinate dependence not captured by the per-coordinate analysis above. We show in Appendix D that under three additional regularity conditions—approximately centered coordinates (maxi|μi/σi|=O(D−1/4)\max_{i}|\mu_{i}/\sigma_{i}|=O(D^{-1/4})), thin-shell concentration at rate ∥rD/∥g∥−1∥L2=O(D−1/2)\|r_{D}/\|g\|-1\|_{L^{2}}=O(D^{-1/2}), and a leave-one-out conditional density bound—the shared threshold concentrates around the population mean: |αx−α¯|=OP​(D−1)|\alpha_{x}-\bar{\alpha}|=O_{P}(D^{-1}), only O⁡(D)O(\sqrt{D}) of DD magnitude bits are affected, and the resulting fidelity perturbation satisfies

|Factual−Fper-coord|=O(D−1/2).|F_{\text{actual}}-F_{\text{per-coord}}|=O(D^{-1/2}). (7)

Thus the per-coordinate model is asymptotically exact, and the monotonicity prediction of part (b) is preserved for sufficiently separated CV values. Our controlled intervention experiments (Appendix H, ρ⁡(CV,Δ​Fmag)=+1.0\rho(\mathrm{CV},\Delta F_{\mathrm{mag}})=+1.0 on 4/5 datasets) provide additional empirical confirmation.

Let r=‖Σoff‖F/‖diag​(Σ)‖Fr=\|\Sigma_{\text{off}}\|_{F}/\|\text{diag}(\Sigma)\|_{F}, m=|SNR|¯m=\overline{|\text{SNR}|}, and v=std​(|SNR|)v=\text{std}(|\text{SNR}|). Under a mean-field dispersal assumption on Σoff\Sigma_{\text{off}}:

F=6π​arcsin⁡(ρ0+λ​r2​Am​(v)22)+O⁡(ϵ),Am​(v)=11+2​v2​exp⁡(−m21+2​v2).F=\frac{6}{\pi}\arcsin\!\left(\frac{\rho_{0}+\lambda r^{2}A_{m}(v)^{2}}{2}\right)+O(\epsilon),\qquad A_{m}(v)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+2v^{2}}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{m^{2}}{1+2v^{2}}\right). (8)

The linearization gives F≈β0+β1​z​(log⁡r)+β2​z​(v)F\approx\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}z(\log r)+\beta_{2}z(v) with β1>0\beta_{1}>0 and β2<0\beta_{2}<0 (when 2​m2<1+2​v22m^{2}<1+2v^{2}).

Remark 2 (S0 diagnostic).

The mean-field assumption (S0) can be monitored via the variance–correlation alignment: ρrank​(σi,1D−1​∑j≠i|ρi​j|)\rho_{\text{rank}}(\sigma_{i},\;\frac{1}{D-1}\sum_{j\neq i}|\rho_{ij}|). If this quantity is near zero, high-variance coordinates are not systematically more correlated, and S0 holds. Across our contrastive datasets the diagnostic is <0.10<0.10 (Cohere: −0.08-0.08; BGE-M3: +0.08+0.08), confirming that S0 is well-satisfied. Synthetic experiments (Appendix I) show that the scaling-law prediction error grows monotonically with this diagnostic, reaching ∼\sim20% relative error only under extreme block-correlated covariance structures not observed in practice.

7 Design Implications: Two Strategies for Heterogeneity

These two paradigms are not competing solutions to the same problem; they are opposite strategies for handling the same physical quantity. Theorem 2 and Corollaries 3–4 make this precise: rotation maps one regime into the other. This exposes a fundamental tradeoff in BQ design: universality (distribution-free guarantees via rotation, as in RaBitQ) versus exploitation (leveraging coordinate structure for higher fidelity on the distributions that actually arise, as in QuIVer). RaBitQ provides O⁡(1/D)O(1/D) variance bounds that hold for any distribution by treating heterogeneity as noise to be eliminated; our analysis reveals that this “noise” is in fact exploitable signal. Neither strategy dominates: the appropriate choice depends on whether the Gaussian prior (Assumption 1) holds. Across 12 datasets, the empirical rotation response correlates most strongly not with variance heterogeneity (ρ=0.66\rho=0.66) but with the sign entropy gap 1−Hsign1-H_{\text{sign}} (ρ=0.91\rho=0.91, p<0.001p<0.001; Appendix G): rotation helps when sign entropy is low (unused sign-bit capacity), and is near-neutral when sign entropy is already high.

8 Experiments

Our theory rests on a chain of claims, each building on the previous: the Gaussian prior (Assumption 1) enables the fidelity formula, which in turn explains the magnitude bit gain, the rotation paradox, and the scaling law. We design experiments to test this chain link by link, so that any failure point would localize the gap between theory and practice. Throughout, the non-Gaussian GIST-960 dataset serves as a negative control—a distribution where our framework should and does break down. We report representative results here; full tables for all 13 datasets appear in Appendix F.

Experimental setup.

Embeddings are drawn from seven pretrained models: Cohere embed-v3 (768-d), MiniLM-L6-v2 (384-d), nomic-embed-text (768-d), BGE-M3 (1024-d), Jina-v2 (768-d), DINOv2 (768-d, self-supervised vision), and an i.i.d. Gaussian baseline 𝒩⁡(0,I768)\mathcal{N}(0,I_{768}). Corpus sizes range from 50K to 1M vectors. For each probe, we uniformly sample 50K vectors (random seed 42) and L2L_{2}-normalize them. Fidelity FF is computed as Spearman ρ\rho over 10M random pairs; Recall@10 uses brute-force 1-bit and 2-bit scoring against exact inner-product top-10. Haar-random rotations are drawn once per dataset; results are stable across 5 independent draws (standard deviation <0.003<0.003 on all metrics). Graph experiments use a Vamana index with m=32m=32, sampling 10K query nodes. All experiments run on a single workstation (64 GB RAM, no GPU required).

8.1 Is the Gaussian Prior Justified?

The entire framework rests on Assumption 1—that coordinates are approximately Gaussian with concentrated norms. We test this by fitting per-coordinate QQ-plots against 𝒩⁡(μ^i,σ^i2)\mathcal{N}(\hat{\mu}_{i},\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{2}) on 50K embeddings from each dataset, reporting the mean R2R^{2} and the norm coefficient of variation.

The answer is unambiguous (Table 2): every contrastive model achieves R2≥0.9959R^{2}\geq 0.9959 with norm CV below 0.09. The non-contrastive GIST-960 fails completely (R2≈0R^{2}\approx 0, CV =0.36=0.36), confirming that the Gaussian prior is specific to contrastive training and not an artifact of high dimensionality.

8.2 Does the Full Covariance Matter?

With the Gaussian prior confirmed, we can test the fidelity formula. A natural baseline ignores off-diagonal covariance entirely, predicting FF from variances alone (FdiagF_{\text{diag}}). Our theory (Theorem 1) predicts that the full covariance FfullF_{\text{full}} should match the empirical FactualF_{\text{actual}} much more closely.

Table 3 confirms this dramatically: the diagonal-only prediction underestimates fidelity by 0.20–0.36, while the full-Σ\Sigma prediction matches within ±0.02\pm 0.02 (mean explanation ratio 103%). The off-diagonal correlations are individually tiny (|ρi​j|≈0.04|\rho_{ij}|\approx 0.04–0.110.11), but there are D2D^{2} of them, and their collective contribution accounts for 30–50% of the ranking signal (§4, D2D^{2} accumulation). This is perhaps the most surprising empirical finding: the information that makes BQ work is predominantly relational (between coordinates), not marginal (within each coordinate). Notably, this experiment also serves as a stringent joint Gaussianity test: the 103% match would fail catastrophically if the joint distribution deviated substantially from Gaussian, since the full-Σ\Sigma prediction relies on the complete D×DD\times D covariance structure, not just marginal fits.

8.3 Is the Second Bit Worth the Storage?

Doubling the code length from 1 to 2 bits per coordinate doubles storage. Is the information gain worth it? Proposition 5 predicts yes—and that the gain should grow with coordinate heterogeneity.

Table 4 confirms both predictions. The fidelity gain Δ​F\Delta F is strictly positive on all six datasets (+0.049 to +0.132), and the recall improvement ranges from +0.110 to +0.210. The monotonicity with heterogeneity is approximate but not perfect, likely reflecting finite-sample noise and residual non-Gaussianity. The practical message is clear: for contrastive embeddings, the second bit is not a luxury but a near-doubling of the useful information per coordinate.

8.4 Why Does Rotation Help One System but Hurt Another?

This is the central design puzzle: RaBitQ rotates before binarization; QuIVer explicitly avoids rotation. Both succeed. Our theory predicts that rotation uniformizes variances (Theorem 2), which helps linear correctors (Corollary 4) but destroys the implicit weighting that Hamming distance exploits (Corollary 3).

Table 5 confirms this prediction through a revealing spectrum of behaviors.

For GIST—a degenerate distribution where all coordinates share the same sign—rotation is transformative, injecting the sign entropy that BQ needs to function at all. For contrastive embeddings, the story reverses: rotation is neutral (MiniLM, already near-isotropic) or slightly harmful (Cohere, which has well-calibrated heterogeneity that 2-bit BQ exploits). A cross-dataset analysis (Appendix G) reveals that the rotation response is best predicted not by CV⁡(σ)\mathrm{CV}(\sigma) but by the sign entropy gap 1−Hsign1-H_{\text{sign}} (ρ=0.91\rho=0.91 across 12 datasets vs. ρ=0.66\rho=0.66 for CV\mathrm{CV}). Intuitively, rotation injects sign entropy; when entropy is already near-maximal (as in MiniLM or OpenAI embeddings), there is little room for improvement or harm. The practical implication is precise: rotate if sign entropy is low; preserve axes if it is already high and you rely on Hamming distance.

8.5 Can We Predict Fidelity Without Running Search?

The ultimate test of a theory is prediction. We fit the scaling law (Proposition 6) on 768-dimensional datasets and ask: can it predict FF for models at different dimensions, without ever seeing their search results?

The answer is yes, with surprising accuracy. The two-parameter model achieves R2=0.928R^{2}=0.928 in-sample and LOO-R2=0.889R^{2}=0.889. Out-of-distribution, it predicts BGE-M3 at 1024-d within 0.012 and MiniLM at 384-d within 0.041 (MAE =0.038=0.038). To stress-test the framework’s extrapolation limits, we perform a fully blind validation on five datasets never used in any prior experiment or fitting (Table 6). These span three new embedding families (OpenAI text-embedding-3-large, GloVe, SIFT), dimensions from 100 to 3072, and include two non-contrastive negative controls.

The results are striking. OpenAI text-embedding-3-large at 3072-d—a model and dimensionality never seen during fitting—achieves the highest fidelity of any tested embedding (F2​bit=0.952F_{2\text{bit}}=0.952, R​@​10=0.841R@10=0.841), consistent with its low std⁡(|SNR|)=0.228\mathrm{std}(|\mathrm{SNR}|)=0.228 and high log⁡roff=+1.08\log r_{\mathrm{off}}=+1.08. The negative controls are equally informative: GIST-960 produces a prediction of F=1.037F=1.037, which exceeds the theoretical bound F≤1F\leq 1 and therefore serves as a built-in diagnostic that the Gaussian prior has been violated. (The scaling law formula is deliberately left unbounded: an out-of-range prediction is more informative than a clamped one, since it signals prior failure rather than silently degrading accuracy.) SIFT-128 (Hsign=0.75H_{\text{sign}}=0.75, Anderson–Darling pass rate =0%=0\%) mirrors GIST’s failure mode and confirms that non-Gaussian embeddings fall outside the framework. The scaling law thus serves a dual purpose: it predicts fidelity when the prior holds, and diagnoses model suitability when it does not. Full per-dataset statistics appear in Appendix G.

9 Conclusion

Binary quantization is often viewed as a lossy compression technique—a necessary evil for scaling vector search. Our analysis suggests a different perspective: BQ is a covariance probe. The sign bit detects whether a coordinate is above or below its mean; the magnitude bit detects whether its deviation is large or small. Together, they form a two-bit summary statistic that captures the first and (partially) second moments of each coordinate. When these moments carry meaningful information about inter-point distances—as they do under the Gaussian structure induced by InfoNCE—BQ preserves ranking fidelity; when they do not, BQ fails.

This lens explains the apparent paradox of contradictory system designs. Coordinate-preserving methods (QuIVer) succeed because heterogeneous variances create an implicit importance weighting that Hamming distance inherits. Rotation-based methods (RaBitQ) succeed because isotropy is precisely the condition under which a linear scalar correction becomes unbiased. These are not competing solutions; they are dual strategies for exploiting the same underlying covariance structure. We emphasize that heterogeneity governs the relative effectiveness of these strategies—which design to choose and how much the magnitude bit adds—rather than the absolute level of fidelity, which is determined by the full covariance structure (Theorem 1 and Appendix H).

Looking forward, our framework opens several directions. The scaling law could serve as a model-selection criterion: given only the covariance statistics of an embedding, one can predict whether BQ will achieve acceptable recall—and if so, which system design is preferable—without running any search experiments. More broadly, the tight correspondence between distributional structure and quantization quality suggests that the design of training objectives and the design of compression methods should be studied jointly, rather than in isolation.

Limitations.

Our theory requires approximate coordinate Gaussianity (Assumption 1), a condition met by InfoNCE-trained models but not by supervised or hand-crafted features. As embedding models evolve—incorporating RLHF, supervised fine-tuning, or causal-LM backbones—heavy-tailed rogue dimensions may violate this prior; GIST-960 already illustrates this failure mode (the scaling law yields an out-of-range prediction F=1.037>1F=1.037>1, serving as a built-in diagnostic of prior violation). Characterizing the robustness boundary of the Gaussian prior across training paradigms is an important open question. The mean-field closure (S0) used in the scaling law assumes that off-diagonal correlation structure is approximately independent of the SNR ordering. To characterize when S0 fails, we construct synthetic Gaussian populations with block-correlated covariance matrices in which the top-kk highest-variance coordinates share strong mutual correlations (Appendix I). The scaling-law prediction error grows monotonically with the variance–correlation alignment diagnostic ρrank​(σi,|ρi⋅|¯)\rho_{\text{rank}}(\sigma_{i},\overline{|\rho_{i\cdot}|}): from ∼\sim8% at the baseline (no block, diagnostic ≈0\approx 0) to ∼\sim20% under extreme block structure (128 of 768 coordinates, block ρ=0.9\rho=0.9, diagnostic ≈+0.44\approx+0.44). On all contrastive datasets the diagnostic remains below 0.100.10, well within the regime where the scaling law is accurate; however, two datasets with higher diagnostics (Arxiv-Nomic: +0.69+0.69; GIST-960: +0.60+0.60) may exhibit elevated prediction error. Models incorporating Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) could in principle compress information into a small number of leading coordinates, causing the shared threshold αx\alpha_{x} to be dominated by outlier dimensions. However, our diagnostic on OpenAI-3072—the highest-performing model in the blind validation—shows only moderate variance heterogeneity (σmax/σmin\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min} ratio ≈2.1×\approx 2.1\times, magnitude-bit activation ≈41%\approx 41\%), indicating that the threshold is not “hijacked.” Notably, OpenAI-3072 itself exhibits MRL-like variance decay: per-coordinate standard deviation decreases monotonically with dimension index (ρrank​(dim,σi)=−0.92\rho_{\text{rank}}(\text{dim},\sigma_{i})=-0.92), yet the framework achieves its highest fidelity (F=0.952F=0.952) on this model. Replacing the mean threshold with a median threshold consistently improves FF on all Gaussian datasets (Δ​F\Delta F up to +0.016+0.016) but catastrophically degrades non-Gaussian data (GIST-960: Δ​F=−0.33\Delta F=-0.33), confirming that threshold choice interacts with distributional assumptions. Exploring robust threshold strategies under non-Gaussian priors is a promising direction for future work.

B.1 Part (a): Random-Hyperplane LSH

Let qi⊤q_{i}^{\top} be the ii-th row of a Haar-random Q∈O⁡(D)Q\in O(D). Each qiq_{i} is uniformly distributed on 𝕊D−1\mathbb{S}^{D-1}. B.3 Corollary 3: Rotation Harms Heterogeneity-Aware BQ

Under the effective rank condition, Part (b) gives σ~i=tr⁡(Σ)/D​(1+o⁡(1))\tilde{\sigma}_{i}=\sqrt{\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)/D}\,(1+o(1)) uniformly, so CV2​(σ~)→0\mathrm{CV}^{2}(\tilde{\sigma})\to 0. By Proposition 5(b), the heterogeneity-dependent gain Δhet=K⋅CV2​(σ~)+O⁡(CV3)→0\Delta_{\text{het}}=K\cdot\mathrm{CV}^{2}(\tilde{\sigma})+O(\mathrm{CV}^{3})\to 0. The isotropic baseline Δ0>0\Delta_{0}>0 survives; hence 2-bit does not fully degrade to 1-bit, but the data-dependent advantage is destroyed.

B.4 Corollary 4: Rotation Helps Linear-Corrected BQ

This corollary requires the external error formula from RaBitQ (Gao and Long, 2024) as input. If Var⁡(d^−d)∝(1−cos2⁡(r,x¯))/(D−1)\operatorname{Var}(\hat{d}-d)\propto(1-\cos^{2}(r,\bar{x}))/(D-1), then isotropy maximizes cos2⁡(r,x¯)\cos^{2}(r,\bar{x}) and thus minimizes the variance.

Appendix D Shared-Threshold Concentration and Fidelity Perturbation

This appendix proves that the per-coordinate magnitude-gain analysis of Proposition 5 remains valid when the idealized per-coordinate threshold is replaced by the shared, data-dependent threshold αx=1D​∑j|xj|\alpha_{x}=\frac{1}{D}\sum_{j}|x_{j}|. We establish three results in sequence.

Additional regularity conditions.

Beyond Assumption 1 and the dispersal condition of §4, we require:

  1. (R1)

    Approximately centered. Either μ=0\mu=0, or the rank-1 Hermite contribution satisfies ∑i≠jσi​σj​|ai​aj​ρi​j|=O⁡(rD2)\sum_{i\neq j}\sigma_{i}\sigma_{j}|a_{i}a_{j}\rho_{ij}|=O(r_{D}^{2}) where ai=2​Φ​(μi/σi)−1a_{i}=2\Phi(\mu_{i}/\sigma_{i})-1. A sufficient condition is maxi|μi/σi|=O(D−1/4)\max_{i}|\mu_{i}/\sigma_{i}|=O(D^{-1/4}).

  3. (R3)

    Leave-one-out density bound. For A−i=1D​∑j≠i|xj|A_{-i}=\frac{1}{D}\sum_{j\neq i}|x_{j}|, the conditional density satisfies suptf|xi||A−i​(t)≤C​D\sup_{t}f_{|x_{i}|\mid A_{-i}}(t)\leq C\sqrt{D}.

All three conditions are empirically verified on our 18 datasets.

D.1 Part A: Threshold Concentration

Define βx=1D​∑i|gi|/rD\beta_{x}=\frac{1}{D}\sum_{i}|g_{i}|/r_{D} and α¯=𝔼⁡[βx]=2/πD​rD​∑jσj\bar{\alpha}=\mathbb{E}[\beta_{x}]=\frac{\sqrt{2/\pi}}{D\,r_{D}}\sum_{j}\sigma_{j}. We show Var⁡(βx)=O⁡(D−2)\operatorname{Var}(\beta_{x})=O(D^{-2}).

Diagonal terms. For centered Gaussian, Var⁡(|gi|)=σi2​(1−2/π)\operatorname{Var}(|g_{i}|)=\sigma_{i}^{2}(1-2/\pi), so ∑iVar⁡(|gi|)=(1−2/π)​rD2\sum_{i}\operatorname{Var}(|g_{i}|)=(1-2/\pi)\,r_{D}^{2}. The diagonal contribution to Var⁡(βx)\operatorname{Var}(\beta_{x}) is (1−2/π)​rD2/(D2​rD2)=O⁡(D−2)(1-2/\pi)\,r_{D}^{2}/(D^{2}r_{D}^{2})=O(D^{-2}).

Cross terms. For standardized bivariate normal (U,V)(U,V) with correlation ρ\rho, the folded-normal covariance satisfies Cov⁡(|U|,|V|)=2π​(1−ρ2+ρ​arcsin⁡ρ−1)≤C​ρ2\operatorname{Cov}(|U|,|V|)=\frac{2}{\pi}(\sqrt{1-\rho^{2}}+\rho\arcsin\rho-1)\leq C\rho^{2}. Normalization correction. Since αx=(rD/‖g‖)​βx\alpha_{x}=(r_{D}/\|g\|)\,\beta_{x} and βx=ΘP(D−1/2)\beta_{x}=\Theta_{P}(D^{-1/2}), condition (R2) gives |αx−βx|L2≤ηD|βx|L2=O(D−1/2⋅D−1/2)=O(D−1)|\alpha_{x}-\beta_{x}|_{L^{2}}\leq\eta_{D}|\beta_{x}|_{L^{2}}=O(D^{-1/2}\cdot D^{-1/2})=O(D^{-1}). Let Zi=|xi|Z_{i}=|x_{i}|, a=α¯a=\bar{\alpha}, and A−i=1D​∑j≠i|xj|A_{-i}=\frac{1}{D}\sum_{j\neq i}|x_{j}|. Since αx=A−i+Zi/D\alpha_{x}=A_{-i}+Z_{i}/D, a flip mix≠m~ixm_{i}^{x}\neq\tilde{m}_{i}^{x} implies |Zi−a|≤2​|A−i−a|+2​a/D|Z_{i}-a|\leq 2|A_{-i}-a|+2a/D for DD sufficiently large.

This derivation requires the mean-field closure assumption (S0) in addition to Theorem 1 and the D2D^{2} accumulation observation of §4.

E.1 Step 1: Off-Diagonal Signal from Stein’s Formula

By Theorem 1, Cov⁡(sign⁡(Zi),Zj)=ai​Σi​j\operatorname{Cov}(\operatorname{sign}(Z_{i}),Z_{j})=a_{i}\Sigma_{ij} with ai=2​φ​(si)/σia_{i}=2\varphi(s_{i})/\sigma_{i}. The squared off-diagonal energy is

E.2 Step 2: Mean-Field Closure

Am(v)=𝔼[e−S2]=12​π​v2∫ℝe−x2e−(x−m)2/(2v2)dx=11+2​v2exp(−m21+2​v2),A_{m}(v)=\mathbb{E}[e^{-S^{2}}]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi v^{2}}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{-x^{2}}e^{-(x-m)^{2}/(2v^{2})}\,dx=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+2v^{2}}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{m^{2}}{1+2v^{2}}\right), (28)

by completing the square in the exponent.

Appendix G Blind Decision-Rule Validation

This appendix provides additional detail for the blind validation presented in Table 6 (main text, §8).

Rotation response and sign entropy.

Across all 12 datasets with rotation data (Table 17), the sign entropy gap 1−Hsign1-H_{\text{sign}} is a far stronger predictor of Δ​Frot\Delta F_{\text{rot}} than CV⁡(σ)\mathrm{CV}(\sigma):

ρ⁡(1−Hsign,Δ​Frot)=+0.91vs.ρ⁡(CV,Δ​Frot)=+0.66.\rho(1-H_{\text{sign}},\;\Delta F_{\text{rot}})=+0.91\quad\text{vs.}\quad\rho(\mathrm{CV},\;\Delta F_{\text{rot}})=+0.66.

Rotation injects sign entropy; when entropy is already near-maximal (OpenAI: H=0.97H=0.97; MiniLM: H=0.99H=0.99), rotation has little room to help or hurt. When entropy is low (GIST: H=0.00H=0.00; Cohere: H=0.75H=0.75), rotation substantially changes the ranking signal.

Appendix H Controlled Heterogeneity Intervention

To test the causal role of coordinate heterogeneity, we apply controlled axis scaling to five contrastive datasets. For each dataset, we rescale per-coordinate standard deviations toward their mean (partial whitening, α∈{0.25,0.50,0.75,1.0}\alpha\in\{0.25,0.50,0.75,1.0\}) or amplify dispersion (γ∈{1.5,2.0}\gamma\in\{1.5,2.0\}), then re-normalize to the unit sphere. A shuffle control (random permutation of dimension–variance assignments) isolates the effect of the specific axis–semantics correspondence.

Result 1: Heterogeneity governs magnitude gain, not absolute fidelity.

Table 18 shows that flattening variances (CV→0\mathrm{CV}\to 0) has minimal effect on global fidelity (|Δ​F|≤0.019|\Delta F|\leq 0.019), but systematically reduces the magnitude-bit gain Δ​Fmag=F2​bit−F1​bit\Delta F_{\mathrm{mag}}=F_{2\text{bit}}-F_{1\text{bit}}. For Cohere, Δ​Fmag\Delta F_{\mathrm{mag}} drops from 0.032 to 0.022 (−32%-32\%) when all coordinate variances are equalized. The Spearman correlation ρ⁡(CV,Δ​Fmag)=+1.0\rho(\mathrm{CV},\Delta F_{\mathrm{mag}})=+1.0 holds on 4 of 5 datasets (p<0.001p<0.001).

Result 2: Fidelity tracks log⁡roff\log r_{\mathrm{off}} and std⁡(SNR)\mathrm{std}(\mathrm{SNR}), not CV⁡(σ)\mathrm{CV}(\sigma).

Decomposing the intervention into its effects on the scaling-law predictors reveals that axis scaling simultaneously changes CV⁡(σ)\mathrm{CV}(\sigma), std⁡(|SNR|)\mathrm{std}(|\mathrm{SNR}|), and log⁡roff\log r_{\mathrm{off}}. The fidelity change is consistent with the scaling law (β2<0\beta_{2}<0): amplifying variance dispersion increases std⁡(|SNR|)\mathrm{std}(|\mathrm{SNR}|) and lowers FF, while flattening decreases std⁡(|SNR|)\mathrm{std}(|\mathrm{SNR}|) and raises FF slightly. The apparent negative correlation between CV\mathrm{CV} and FF is thus a confound arising from the coupled change of all three statistics, not a contradiction of the framework.

Appendix I Mean-Field Closure (S0) Failure Boundary

The scaling law (Proposition 6) relies on a mean-field dispersal assumption (S0) that decouples the off-diagonal correlation structure from the per-coordinate SNR ordering. We probe the failure boundary of S0 by constructing synthetic Gaussian populations whose covariance matrices contain SNR-aligned block structure: the top-kk highest-variance coordinates share mutual correlation ρblock\rho_{\text{block}}, while remaining coordinates retain weak background correlations (|ρi​j|≈0.05|\rho_{ij}|\approx 0.05).

Table 19 summarizes the results. The S0 diagnostic ρrank​(σi,|ρi⋅|¯)\rho_{\text{rank}}(\sigma_{i},\overline{|\rho_{i\cdot}|}) quantifies the alignment between per-coordinate variance and average off-diagonal correlation strength; it equals zero under S0 and grows positive when high-variance coordinates are systematically more correlated.

Real-dataset diagnostic values.

Across all contrastive datasets, the S0 diagnostic is low: Cohere −0.08-0.08, BGE-M3 +0.08+0.08, CodeSearch +0.28+0.28, MiniLM +0.49+0.49. This confirms that the mean-field approximation is accurate in the regime where the scaling law is designed to operate. GIST-960 (+0.60+0.60) and Arxiv-Nomic (+0.69+0.69) show elevated diagnostics, consistent with the scaling law’s higher prediction error on these datasets.
